claims.text: Catalytic activity in transition-metal catalysts is primarily governed by the availability of low-coordinated surface sites.
Reducing nanoparticle size increases the proportion of low-coordinated atoms.
Increasing the proportion of low-coordinated atoms enhances catalytic activity.
A controlled reduction in average nanoparticle size will increase the relative abundance of low-coordinated sites when metal loading and support are held constant.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher density of low-coordinated surface sites than the baseline nanoparticles.
Low-coordinated atoms offer stronger reactant binding or more favorable adsorption geometries.
The binding or adsorption properties of low-coordinated atoms lower the reaction activation barrier.
Lowering the activation barrier through low-coordinated sites enhances turnover frequency.
Under identical reaction conditions, the smaller-nanoparticle catalyst will exhibit a higher turnover frequency than the baseline catalyst.
The proposed size-activity relationship should hold for single-phase transition-metal catalysts on inert supports under the specified reaction conditions.
The proposed relationship may not apply to complex alloys or catalysts containing promoter elements.
The magnitude of the turnover-frequency increase varies with the reaction and the intrinsic properties of the metal.
Dominant support interactions could prevent the expected turnover-frequency increase.
